text.en: Meena read the words liberty, equality, fraternity. "Where did they come from?" she asked.

The age of revolutions changed the world. The American Revolution (1776) freed thirteen colonies from Britain, and the Declaration of Independence spoke of equal rights. The French Revolution (1789) began against the king's rule and high taxes and declared liberty, equality and fraternity.
Napoleon rose to power in France and spread revolutionary ideas, but he was defeated at Waterloo in 1815. The Latin American countries won independence from Spain and Portugal under leaders such as Simon Bolivar.
These revolutions inspired people everywhere to demand rights and ended old monarchies in many places.
The age of revolutions changed the world.
The American Revolution (1776) freed thirteen colonies from Britain, and the Declaration of Independence spoke of equal rights.
The French Revolution (1789) began against the king's rule and high taxes and declared liberty, equality and fraternity.
Napoleon rose to power in France and spread revolutionary ideas, but he was defeated at Waterloo in 1815.
The Latin American countries won independence from Spain and Portugal under leaders such as Simon Bolivar.
These revolutions inspired people everywhere to demand rights and ended old monarchies in many places.
During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, Enlightenment thinkers like John Locke, Montesquieu and Rousseau argued that governments exist by consent of the governed, not divine right of kings.
Montesquieu proposed dividing government into Legislature, Executive and Judiciary so no single ruler could become a tyrant—an idea later built into modern constitutions including India's.
Rousseau's 'Social Contract' opened with the bold claim that people are born free and sovereign authority belongs to the citizens.
These ideas first sparked fire in North America, where thirteen British colonies resented British taxes like the Stamp Act and Tea Act imposed without colonial representation in Parliament.
In 1773, protesters dumped chests of taxed tea into Boston Harbor in the famous Boston Tea Party, escalating tensions into the American War of Independence.
On 4 July 1776, Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence, proclaiming that all people are created equal with rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
Led by General George Washington and aided by France, the colonies defeated Britain at Yorktown, winning recognition in the Treaty of Paris (1783) and adopting a federal Constitution.
Across the Atlantic, France faced a deep crisis under King Louis XVI. Society was split into Three Estates: the First Estate (Clergy) and Second Estate (Nobility) paid almost no taxes.

board.text: France's Three Estates: unequal tax burden

text.en: The Third Estate—peasants, artisans, shopkeepers and lawyers making up over ninety-five percent of France—paid heavy taxes while suffering bread shortages and costly royal wars.

board.text: Third Estate bore the entire tax burden

text.en: When Louis XVI called the Estates-General in 1789, the Third Estate broke away to form the National Assembly and swore the Tennis Court Oath to write a constitution.
On 14 July 1789, angry Parisians stormed the Bastille prison-fortress, a symbol of royal tyranny—a date still celebrated as France's Bastille Day.
The National Assembly abolished feudal dues and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, championing Liberty, Equality and Fraternity.
Soon France became a republic, King Louis XVI was executed, and during the Reign of Terror (1793–94) Robespierre's radical committee used the guillotine against suspected enemies.
Chaos paved the way for brilliant general Napoleon Bonaparte, who took power in 1799 and crowned himself Emperor in 1804, spreading the Napoleonic Code of legal equality across Europe.
Although Napoleon was finally defeated at Waterloo in 1815, Europe could never return completely to absolute feudal monarchy; constitutional and nationalist ideals had taken root.
Meanwhile, in Latin America, inspired by the American and French Revolutions, leaders like Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín led colonies to throw off Spanish and Portuguese rule.
Haiti achieved a historic triumph in 1804, led by Toussaint Louverture, becoming the first independent republic born from a successful uprising of enslaved people.

These revolutions also echoed in India: leaders from Raja Ram Mohan Roy to Tipu Sultan followed French revolutionary ideals closely, and India's Constitution later adopted Liberty, Equality and Fraternity in its Preamble!
Notice how the two revolutions differed: the American Revolution was an anti-colonial struggle for self-rule, while the French Revolution overturned a centuries-old feudal class system from within.
Both revolutions had limits at first—women and enslaved people had to keep fighting for decades to win full voting rights—proving democracy is an ongoing journey.

board.text: Early limits: long struggle for full equality

text.en: Written constitutions, bills of rights, elected parliaments and equality before the law all trace directly back to this Age of Revolutions.
Timeline check: 1773 Boston Tea Party -> 1776 American Independence -> 1789 Bastille -> 1804 Napoleon & Haiti -> 1815 Waterloo.
To analyse any revolution, look for three sparks: economic hardship or unfair taxes, inspiring new ideas, and a trigger event like the Tea Party or Bastille.
The Age of Revolutions replaced subjects of kings with citizens of nations—shaping the democratic world we live in today.

board.text: From royal subjects to free citizens

problem.en: Why did the Third Estate break away from France's Estates-General in 1789 to form the National Assembly?

text.en: Look at the voting rule in the Estates-General.

why.en: Each Estate had only one collective vote, so the privileged First and Second Estates could always outvote the Third Estate two to one.

text.en: Look at who paid the taxes.

why.en: The Third Estate represented over 95% of France's population and paid nearly all taxes, yet had no fair say in reforms.

text.en: Connect this to the Tennis Court Oath.

why.en: Demanding 'one member, one vote', Third Estate deputies formed the National Assembly to write a constitution representing the people.
